Complete Empirical Research Plan

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Preferred strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension.

Why it is appropriate
•  The arbitration award date sharply separates a clearly defined pre-period (contract still in force) from a post-period (new wage implemented).  
•  Within the 9 % of bargaining rounds that reach arbitration, whether the union “wins” (its offer is picked) or “loses” (municipality’s lower offer is picked) is plausibly as-good-as-random conditional on observables because the arbitrator must choose one entire offer and cannot split the difference.  
•  We observe untreated police departments (arbitration cases where the union wins or non-arbitrating municipalities) that furnish a credible counterfactual trend.  
•  Monthly panel data permit municipality and month-year fixed effects, satisfying the usual DID requirements and allowing an event-study pre-trend test.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 for municipality-months in which the new wage came from an arbitration loss by the union, yielding a raise below the union’s requested raise.  

Continuous dosage variable  
shortfall_pct = (Union offer – Award) in percentage-point terms; 0 if union wins. We will interact this with Post.

Control groups  
A. Within-arbitration control: municipalities that went to arbitration but where the union won.  
B. External control: municipalities that never entered arbitration in the same calendar years (placebo check).

Treatment timing  
event_time = 0 in the award month; Post = 1 starting the first full month after award, staying 1 until the next contract expires or until the panel ends.

(No running variable/cut-off needed because we do not implement an RDD.)

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of an arbitration shortfall, productivity outcomes in loser and winner municipalities would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: Arbitration is compulsory once triggered; the specific outcome (win vs loss) hinges on a third-party arbitrator, not the officers, supporting parallel trends. We will test with leads in the event study.

A2. No anticipation: Officers cannot perfectly predict arbitration outcomes and do not alter behavior before the decision.  
Plausibility: Offers are simultaneously revealed to the arbitrator only late in the process; exact selection is unknown ex ante.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers): A union’s loss does not affect officers in other municipalities.  
Plausibility: Municipal police departments operate independently, and officers rarely move across departments in a month or two.

A4. Exogenous timing: The calendar month in which the award is announced is not chosen to coincide with productivity shocks.  
Plausibility: Statutory timeline (120/60-day rules) largely fixes timing.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Major Threats and Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
Threat 1: Selection into arbitration (only contentious negotiations arbitrate).  
Fix: Include municipality fixed effects and limit analysis to the subset of municipalities that at least once reached arbitration, using winner cases as the counterfactual; add controls for pre-award crime trends and economic covariates.

Threat 2: Anticipatory effort changes (moral hazard while award is pending).  
Fix: Incorporate leads of treatment in the event-study graph; drop 3–4 months immediately before the award in robustness checks.

Threat 3: Correlated shocks (budget cuts, simultaneous staffing changes).  
Fix: Control for time-varying covariates: municipal unemployment, population, seasonal dummies, officer headcount. Add municipality-specific linear trends in robustness.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)        # panel DID regressions
library(ggplot2)       # event-study plots

# 1. Load Data --------------------------------------------------------------
ucr  <- fread("ucr_monthly_1976_1996.csv")       # municipality-month
perc <- fread("perc_arbitrations_1978_1995.csv") # one row per case
obts <- fread("obts_1989_1990.csv")              # arrestee level

# 2. Construct Arbitration Variables ---------------------------------------
perc[, union_win    := (award_side == "union")]
perc[, shortfall_pct:= ifelse(union_win, 0,
                              union_offer_pct - award_pct)]      # positive if loss
# Expand arbitration data to months ----------------------------------------
# Assume perc has start_month (yyyy-mm) and end_month of prior contract
arb_mo <- perc[, .(municipality_id,
                   event_date = as.IDate(award_month),
                   union_win,
                   shortfall_pct)]
ucr[, month_id := as.IDate(paste0(year, "-", month, "-01"))]

ucr <- merge(ucr, arb_mo, by = "municipality_id", all.x = TRUE)

# 3. Treatment timing -------------------------------------------------------
ucr[, post := ifelse(!is.na(event_date) & month_id > event_date, 1, 0)]
ucr[, treat := post * (union_win == 0)]                      # 1 only for losers post
ucr[, treat_cont := post * shortfall_pct]                    # continuous dosage

# Keep only municipalities that ever arbitrated for baseline specification
ucr_arb <- ucr[!is.na(event_date)]

# 4. Main DID Regression ----------------------------------------------------
did1 <- feols(arrests_total ~ treat | municipality_id + month_id, 
              data = ucr_arb, cluster = ~municipality_id)
summary(did1)

# Continuous dosage specification
did2 <- feols(arrests_total ~ treat_cont | municipality_id + month_id, 
              data = ucr_arb, cluster = ~municipality_id)
summary(did2)

# 5. Event-Study ------------------------------------------------------------
ucr_arb[, rel_month := as.integer((month_id - event_date)/30.4)]
ucr_arb[, rel_month_grp := fifelse(rel_month < -24, -24,
                           fifelse(rel_month > 36, 36, rel_month))]

es <- feols(arrests_total ~ i(rel_month_grp, union_win==0) | 
            municipality_id + month_id, data = ucr_arb,
            cluster = ~municipality_id)

iplot(es, ref.line =  -0.5) + ggtitle("Event-study: Arrests")

# 6. Robustness: Add non-arbitrating municipalities ------------------------
ucr[, ever_arbitrated := !is.na(event_date)]
did_rb <- feols(arrests_total ~ post*lose | municipality_id + month_id,
                data = ucr, cluster = ~municipality_id)
# where lose = 1 if union ever loses and the municipality is in loser post period

```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Prediction: Officers who receive a smaller-than-expected raise will reduce effort (“partial shirking”).  
Magnitude: Prior work on reference-dependent effort suggests 1–3 % declines in high-frequency productivity when pay falls short of a salient reference point. I expect:  
• Arrests and clearances ↓ 2 %–4 % in the first 12 months.  
• No meaningful change when the union wins.  
• Effect size proportional to shortfall: roughly −0.5 pp arrest rate per 1 pp wage shortfall.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Pre-trend equivalence tested and passes ………………… 1  
C2: No simultaneous confounders unaccounted for ………… 0.5  
C3: Precise treatment timing (sharp intervention) ………… 1  
C4: No interference between units ………………………………… 0.5  
C5: Common outcome measurement across groups ………… 1  
TOTAL (out of 5) ………………………………………… 4.0

────────────────────────────────────────
End of Plan
